manifest.name: dsh-journal
manifest.description: Graded long-term memory as a first-class DeepSeek Harness tool: entries carry a level, an expiry and a review date, so the right things persist for the right amount of time.

bundle.text:
# dsh-journal bundle layer: one row mounting the `journal` tool over the
# graded long-term log. The store lives outside the profile on D: on purpose -
# every profile on this machine shares it, and it must never land in whatever
# directory the harness happened to start in.
- insert:
    - id: journal
      name: 'dsh-journal'
      config:
        root: 'D:/dsh-data/journal'

readme.text: A DeepSeek Harness plugin that turns a plain JSONL file into a first-class `journal` tool with graded memory: entries carry a level, an expiry, and a review date, so a long-lived assistant can remember the right things for the right amount of time — and let the rest go on its own.

A single undifferentiated memory file fails in two directions at once. Keep everything and the useful part drowns; keep only recent things and the relationship and the standing preferences — the parts that make an assistant feel like the same person — are exactly what gets dropped.

So every entry gets one of four levels, and the level decides its lifetime:

| level | meaning | lifetime |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `S` | relationship, emotion, shared experience, promises | never auto-deleted; pinned |
| `A` | durable facts, preferences, key decisions | 365 days |
| `B` | project context, task progress | 60 days |
| `C` | transient details, one-off operations | 7 days |

`prune` soft-deletes expired rows into `archive/`; nothing is ever physically removed by the tool. Pinned rows are exempt.

The useful question when writing is not "is this important" but **"which of these is this, a skeleton or a file"** — the rules for how someone talks to you belong in `S`, the port number you debugged yesterday belongs in `B`, and a handoff note for the next session belongs in `A` because it only needs to survive until you read it.

| action | does |
| --- | --- |
| `add` | write one entry (`level`, `title`, `text` required) |
| `list` | list entries, optionally by level / status |
| `search` | substring search across title, text and tags |
| `digest` | the `S` + `A` summary — what a fresh session should read first |
| `stats` | counts per level, size, expired-but-present |
| `review` | push one entry's expiry out |
| `prune` | soft-delete everything past its expiry |
| `render` | rewrite `JOURNAL.md` as a readable digest |

Typical use in an agent loop:

```
journal action=digest                          # at the start of every new conversation
journal action=add level=S title="..." text="..."
journal action=search query=备考
journal action=prune dryRun=true               # see what would expire, change nothing

One JSON object per line at `<root>/journal.jsonl`. Writes go through a temp file and a rename, so a crash mid-write cannot tear the store. A torn trailing line on read is skipped rather than failing the call.

Row shape:

```json
{
  "id": "j-20261104-140902-479d",
  "ts": "2026-11-04T14:09:02+00:00",
  "level": "B",

The format is deliberately plain. Any script that can read JSONL can read this, and any script that can write one line can add to it.

A DeepSeek Harness plugin only receives the host packages (`@deepseek-ai/*`) when it is installed as a **link**. An ordinary npm dependency fails to import and is silently skipped.

Configuration (in the bundle layer `cordis.patch.yml`):

| key | default | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `root` | `D:/dsh-data/journal` (Windows) / `/dsh-data/journal` | where `journal.jsonl` lives |
| `toolName` | `journal` | the tool's name in the model's toolset |

`JOURNAL_ROOT` overrides `root` from the environment.

```bash
node _selftest.mjs
```

Runs against a temporary store: add at each level, list, search, digest, stats, prune dry-run, render, review, and the two validation paths (bad level, empty title are both rejected).

readme.section: Note on what it is not
readme.text: This is not a vector store and does not do retrieval by similarity. It is a small, inspectable, hand-curated log — closer to a notebook than a database. The bet is that an assistant which writes down the right few hundred lines, and forgets the rest on schedule, beats one that hoards everything and searches it.
